title: Dissecting Multimodal In-Context Learning
one_liner: Transformers learn to associate information across modalities by copying labels from matching examples, but they do it unevenly—the secondary modality (like captions) learns from very few examples when trained on diverse primary data (like images).
lead: Modern transformers can learn new tasks from a handful of examples inside a single prompt—this ability is called in-context learning. But when a transformer sees both images and text, how does it learn to link them together? This paper traces the hidden wiring: transformers use an induction mechanism (a built-in pattern-matching circuit) to find examples that look similar and copy their labels. The asymmetry is the surprise: the secondary modality (e.g., text descriptions) requires far less diversity than the primary modality (e.g., the image collection) for this to work.

problem.h2: Multimodal transformers work, but we do not know how they learn across modalities
paras: When you train a transformer on pairs of images and captions, the model learns to associate them—give it a new image and it can generate a caption. But inside the transformer, how does this association actually happen? Is it a mystery or a mechanism we can trace?

A beginner might guess that each modality (vision, language) develops separate pathways and they somehow merge at the end. But this breaks because the model needs to learn associations from just a few examples, and random merging would need a lot of alignment. The real question is: what wiring does the model discover to link new images and captions in a single prompt?

callout.html: How does a transformer learn to match a new image to a new caption label using only a handful of in-context examples?

object.h2: The one thing this paper traces
paras: The paper does not propose a new method—it reverse-engineers an existing one. It reveals that transformers, when trained on multimodal data, automatically develop a hidden mechanism (a built-in wiring) that matches examples and copies their labels across modalities. The object is: attention patterns that find similar earlier examples in the context and relay their labels to the new input.
object.object: attention patterns that match and copy labels

hidden.h2: Learning asymmetry: how much complexity each modality needs
hidden.name: modality complexity asymmetry
paras: The paper measures a surprising asymmetry: when training on multimodal data, the secondary modality (e.g., captions) requires much lower data complexity than the primary modality (e.g., images) for in-context learning to emerge. Complexity here means diversity—how many different distinct types of data the model sees.

They discover this by controlling the statistics of synthetic data: training on high-diversity images but low-diversity captions still allows the transformer to learn the cross-modal link in-context. This challenges the intuition that both modalities need equal training richness.

heat.caption: Darker means more data complexity needed. Primary modality needs high diversity; secondary modality needs surprisingly little.

reads.html: If you train a transformer on 1000 different image types but only 10 different captions, it still learns to match new images to captions from in-context examples. The captions do not need diversity.

The paper controls how varied the task examples are and modality-specific data complexity in synthetic experiments, finding that the secondary modality can remain low-variety while the primary modality scales high-variety, yet multimodal in-context learning still emerges via matching circuits.

mechanism.h2: How transformers copy labels across modalities
paras: The transformer builds two linked attention patterns. The first scans the primary modality (images) to find which earlier examples resemble the current input, comparing low-level features like color and shape. This is the matching head—a pattern-comparison circuit. Once it identifies the matching earlier example, the second pattern grabs the label attached to that example. Because the matching head does the hard work of finding the match using varied image features, the secondary modality only needs to store the association—it does not need its own diversity to learn the link. The primary modality's high diversity makes the matching reliable; the secondary modality just tags along.

Critically, both modalities refine their circuits together during training: the visual matching circuit and the caption-copying circuit co-evolve. But the visual side carries the load of learning to discriminate examples, so the caption side can be learned from fewer distinct types.

stages.s: Image plus caption, repeated examples, then new image
Matching head compares visual features of new image to earlier images
Attention identifies the most similar earlier example
Label-copying head retrieves caption from the matched example
Predicted caption for the new image

math.words: For each prior example in the context, compute a similarity score based on how much its image resembles the current input image. Normalize these scores so they sum to one (they become weights). Then take a weighted sum of the prior captions using these weights. The transformer learns both the similarity scoring function and when to use it.
math.equation: output_label = sum_j weight_j * prior_caption_j, where weight_j = softmax_j(similarity(current_image, prior_image_j))

bars.h2: Comparing unimodal and multimodal in-context learning

charts.title: Unimodal (images only)
charts.note: Without captions to anchor associations, image-only models require extensive diversity to learn in-context.

charts.title: Multimodal (images + captions)
charts.note: With multimodal training, captions enable the model to learn associations even when caption data has low diversity, because images carry the discriminative load.

items.html: If the primary modality has low diversity and the secondary modality has high diversity, multimodal induction learning breaks. The induction mechanism cannot match examples if the primary modality lacks discriminative features.

The paper finds that RoPE (a way of labeling where each word sits in the sequence) can delay the emergence of matching circuits, requiring more training time, because RoPE's encoding makes it harder for attention to directly compare positions between examples. Models using other position-labeling methods develop in-context learning faster because their encodings make position comparisons more direct.

The mechanism only works if both modalities describe the same underlying concepts. If captions describe things the images do not show (or vice versa), the induction circuit fails because matching is impossible.

The circuit works when the primary modality provides high feature diversity (many distinct types), the secondary modality provides label associations, and both are aligned on the same concepts. The model then learns in-context associations from just a few examples.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small transformer on synthetic data: generate 50 random images (each is a pattern: striped, dotted, solid; in red, blue, or green). Create labels with low diversity: only 3 captions (red, blue, green). Train on 100 image-caption pairs. At test time, present three in-context examples and a new image, then measure whether the model predicts the correct caption. The experiment proves the asymmetry: this low-diversity caption setup succeeds because the image diversity is high.
demo.closing: The demo must show that accuracy exceeds 75 percent even though captions have only 3 types, proving that multimodal induction learning relies on primary modality diversity, not balanced data complexity.
